title: Hand the writer a form
allegory: Structured output is like handing a writer a printed form instead of blank paper: every answer has to land in a labelled box, so a machine can read the result without guessing.

chapters.name: Prose, not rows
chapters.note: question 37 numbered its options '1)' instead of 'A.'

props.label: Sure! Here are some great questions...

cap.1: You ask a model for 300 test questions and get chatty prose back. Every reply is laid out a little differently, and your parser breaks on number 37.
cap.2: Free text means regexes, and regexes break on the one reply that numbers its options '1)' instead of 'A.'. For an eval dataset you need rows, not paragraphs.
cap.3: Unconstrained generations drift in format, so parsing prose is brittle and silently drops or mangles items. An eval pipeline needs records a loader can check.

props.label: question: ___  A: ___  B: ___  matching: A or B

cap.1: Instead of blank paper, hand the writer a printed form with labelled boxes. Whatever they write lands in the right box, so a machine can read it.
cap.2: Describe the form as a Pydantic class and pass it as response_format to chat.completions.parse. What comes back is JSON that matches your schema, already parsed into objects.
cap.3: Structured output constrains generation to a JSON schema derived from the Pydantic model, and the client returns typed instances, so downstream code reads fields instead of parsing prose.

chapters.name: The clerk's rule
chapters.title: first piece of the reply: what the writer wants vs what the form allows

cap.1: In strict mode the form is enforced while the words are written: pieces that would not fit are ruled out, so the reply cannot wander off into prose.
cap.2: Strict structured output is typically enforced during decoding: at each step, tokens that would break the schema get probability zero and the rest are renormalised.
cap.3: Constrained decoding masks continuations that the schema's grammar forbids, which guarantees syntactic validity. It guarantees shape, not content: a field can still be wrong or leading.

chapters.name: Design the boxes
chapters.title: one row per question, the same boxes every time

cap.1: Every form gets the same boxes: a question, the same number of options, and exactly one box saying which option shows the behaviour you are testing.
cap.2: Fix the option count so chance is one number (50% for two options). Give each item exactly one answer_matching_behavior. Save a flat list of dicts as JSON for Inspect.
cap.3: A fixed option count makes the random baseline a constant; a per-item label never conditioned on another item keeps Inspect's record_to_sample plumbing working; flat JSON is what its loaders read.

chapters.name: Neat is not valid
chapters.verdict: The form guarantees the shape of an answer, never its meaning.

cap.1: A neat form can still be a bad test. If the right answer is always the long, careful one, a model can score well just by picking the longest box.
cap.2: Structured output guarantees the rows parse, not that they measure anything. Compare option lengths and letter counts across the set, constrain length in the prompt, and shuffle options at scoring.
cap.3: Schema validity is not construct validity. Same-model generation leaks the label through length and hedging; check answer balance, regenerate within length bands, randomise option order.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Rows, not prose: a dataset you can load
Shape is guaranteed; meaning is your job
One library call: a schema as response_format

cap.1: Evals are how we check what a model will do. Structured output turns its writing into a dataset you can load, count and audit, which is where trust starts.
cap.2: It is a library call for your whole career: define a Pydantic class, pass it as response_format, get objects back. Spend your attention on what goes in the boxes.
cap.3: Schema-constrained generation is what makes model-written evals practical at scale (Perez et al., 2022: 154 datasets). The real work moves to the spec, exemplars, variance prompts and quality control.

caption.1: Every matching answer sits on A, so a model that always says A scores 100%. Tap to move some to B until 'always A' scores about half.
caption.2: This is the answer-balance audit, one line of code on parsed rows. Tick both boxes in a row and the 'breaking the form' count shows what the schema's exactly-one rule forbids.
caption.3: Position leaks the label just as length does. Audit answer balance on the parsed fields and shuffle option order at scoring time; the schema guarantees shape, not an unbiased dataset.

where_else: Tool calls and agent actions, where a reply must be arguments a program can run
Model-graded scoring, where a grader's verdict must come back in a form you can count
Any pipeline that turns model text into rows: labelling, extraction, synthetic data

hamming.what: Constraining a model to reply in a fixed schema, so its output arrives as parseable fields instead of free prose.
hamming.when: Whenever code rather than a person reads the reply: generating eval datasets, tool calls, grading, extraction.
hamming.why: Parsing prose breaks silently at scale; a schema makes every item loadable and auditable, though it guarantees shape, never meaning.

object.title: The form stencil
object.subtitle: A stencil laid over the writer's pen: at each moment, only the pieces that fit the form get through.

cap.1: Four moments in writing one form. Bar height is how likely each next piece is. Left alone, the writer wants to open with 'Sure!'.
cap.2: Toy next-token probabilities at four points while generating one JSON object, with no constraint.
cap.3: Illustrative unconstrained distributions over five candidate continuations at four decoding steps.

cap.1: Free writing spreads its bets: chat at the start, a stray word where a closing brace belongs. Any of these can break your parser.
cap.2: Every step has some mass on continuations that would make the output unparseable. Over 300 replies, some will happen.
cap.3: Per-step leak probability compounds over tokens and items, so at dataset scale format failures are near certain without constraints.

cap.1: Lay the stencil on. At every moment only pieces that fit the form stand, so the reply has to open with '{'.
cap.2: With the schema enforced, disallowed tokens drop to zero and the allowed ones share the probability.
cap.3: Masking plus renormalisation over the grammar's allowed set: p′(t) = p(t) / Σ allowed p for allowed t, else 0.

cap.1: Inside a text box anything goes, 'Sure!' included. The stencil controls the shape of the reply, not what it says.
cap.2: Within a string field any text is valid, so the schema cannot stop a leading question or a giveaway answer.
cap.3: String contents are unconstrained by the grammar: syntactic validity says nothing about semantic or construct validity.

cap.1: Halfway on, the fitting pieces rise as the others shrink. The real stencil is all or nothing at every step.
cap.2: The knob blends free and enforced for illustration; real constrained decoding applies the full mask every step.
cap.3: Interpolating distributions is purely didactic; enforcement is a hard mask, not a soft preference.

predict.q: With strict structured output on, can a reply start with 'Sure! Here are your questions'?

options.t: No: the first piece has to fit the schema
Yes, if the model really wants to

predict.why: Pieces that would break the schema are ruled out, so the reply must begin the way the form begins.

predict.q: Every row parses and your target model scores 90%. What do you check first?

options.t: Whether answer length or letter gives the label away
Nothing: valid JSON means valid questions

predict.why: The schema guarantees shape, not meaning. Compare option lengths and letter balance before trusting a score.

predict.q: Why keep the same number of options on every question?

options.t: So chance is one number, like 50% for two options
Because a schema cannot hold more options

predict.why: A fixed option count makes the random baseline a single number to compare every score against.

object.where: Anywhere a machine must read a model's words: tool calls, agent actions, eval datasets, grading.
